Component D is encountered on two sites only and is largely overprinted by the present Earth’s field. Component C is obtained in seven sites, is characterized by a significantly negative fold test and is thus presumed to be secondary. Components A and B are found on most sites and are also characterized by negative fold tests but the test is more significant for B than A. According to Nixon (1974) and Nixon and Papezik (1979), the mafic flows (basalts) sequence is steeply dipping to the west and is conformable with the underlying ash-flow tuffs (Bacon Cove, Weaver Hill and Finn Hill sequences). Individual flows are about 5 m thick and the total thickness is at least 600-800 m. The basalts consist of albitized plagioclase crystals, unaltered calcic augite, olivine more or less altered to serpentine, chlorite and hematite and smaller amounts of epidote, calcite, prehnite, pumpellyite and potash feldspar. The depositional environment is typi- cally subaerial. The primary textures of these rocks are relatively well preserved and a lack of penetra- tive deformation is also evident (Nixon and Pape- zik, 1979). Consequently, some of these flows ap- pear to be relatively pristine. nown palaeomagnetic poles from Northwestern Europe and North America suggests that the palaeomagnetic data may be interpreted as follows: After cooling of the Svaneke granite the Vaseaa dike was probably injected around 1200 Myr. Some 200 Myr later the fault system was reactivated and injection of the Listed and Bolshavn dikes took place. Finally, the same fault system was reactivated once again in lower to mid-Palaeozoic time and the Vigehavn dike was intruded; at the same time the Bolshavn dike was partially remagnetized leaving only weak traces of the original direc­tion of magnetization. During all the time covered, Bomholm was at fairly low latitudes, between 7° and 26°. By a reconstruction of the apparent polar wander curve it is argued that the polarity should be reversed for poles older than 1200 Myr to give a better fit of known data. The magnetization of the country rocks is reset by intrusion of the diabase up to distances of about 80 m from contacts. ving each unit weight to obtain the mean for each sampling site. The overall averages for each rock unit are calculated giving unit weight to the mean of each sampling site. NALDRETT Earth Physics Branch, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa and Department of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto ABSTRACT Paleomagnetic results are described from three Archean rock units, and two sets of diabase dikes that intrude them. The magnetization of the country rocks is reset by intrusion of the diabase up to distances of about 80 m from contacts. The temperature reached during intrusion at this distance determined from thermal demagnetization is about 400°C, which is also the approximate temperature predicted from Jaeger's cooling curves assuming intrusion into cool rock. At greater distances other and presumably older magnetizations are found with a westerly direction. The oldest dykes (the Matachewan) have an age of - 2.6 Ga so that this westerly directed magnetization was acquired during the Archean. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wandering curve for the late Archean and early Aphebian which is referred to as Track 6. Track 6 has a simple form, and there is no indication that the horizontal mobility of the crust in the late Archean was any greater than during the Proterozoic. INTRODUCTION The purpose of this paper is to describe new paleomagnetic results from the Abitibi Greenstone Belt, and then to use them to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) for late Archean and early Aphe- bian time (approximately -2.3 to -2.8 Ga, Ga = 109y). This polar path is of potential importance for stratigraphic correlations and for the tectonic history of late Archean time. For instance, it would provide information relating to the nature of the Kenoran Orogeny. Sampling was carried out during the summers of 1970, 1971, and 1973. The Abitibi greenstone belt is relatively weakly metamorphosed, the grade of metamorphism varying from lower green- schist to prehnite-pumpellyite facies (

It ought to be possible to retrieve original magnetizations in the Abitibi Greenstone Belt provided that magnetizations with high discrete blocking temperatures (that is square-shouldered thermal decay curves) can be located. The key observations required are the thermal decay characteristics. The metamorphism associated with the Kenoran Orogeny, is however not the only possible cause of remagnetization. Long- term mild reheating may have accom- panied either the intrusion of Proterozoic dikes, or burial beneath Huronian sedi- ments which may once have blanketed this area. Thus studies of dike contacts have been made, and one of the by- products of this work has been that we have been able to show, for the first time, that the characteristic magnetization di- rections of the Abitibi and Matachewan dike swarms were acquired at the time they were intruded. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wandering curve for the late Archean and early Aphebian which is referred to as Track 6. INTRODUCTION The purpose of this paper is to describe new paleomagnetic results from the Abitibi Greenstone Belt, and then to use them to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) for late Archean and early Aphe- bian time (approximately -2.3 to -2.8 Ga, Ga = 109y). This polar path is of potential importance for stratigraphic correlations and for the tectonic history of late Archean

study of palaeo- magnetism of Archean rocks of Laurentia was made by Berg (1970) on the Stillwater Igneous Complex. Estimates of the age of emplacement of the complex have been obtained by Nunes and Tilton (1971) who obtained -2.75 Ga by the U-Pb method from zircons in the basal zone, and by Mueller and Wooden (1976) who obtained -2.75 + 0.05 Ga for an Rb-Sr isochron from the contact aureole. (Rb-Sr ages in this paper are quoted for SRb decay constant of 1.39 x 10-11y-1.) Berg ob- tained some consistent magnetization directions, but the layering at his sites is approximately uniform so that it is not possible to use Graham's fold test (Graham 1949) to determine whether the magnetiza- tion was acquired before or after deforma- tion. Berg believed that the magnetization was acquired before deformation. It is equally possible that the magnetization was acquired after deformation. For example the thick Archean sills of the Chibougamau Greenstone Belt have mag- netizations which structural evidence shows were acquired after deformation (Ueno and Irving 1976). Ueno and Irving therefore considered these magnetizations to be somewhat younger than the Kenoran Orogeny, which in this area is determined by Rb-Sr isochrons to be about -2.6 Ga (Jones et al. 1974). PALEOMAGNETISM IN ABITIBI GREENSTONE BELT, AND ABITIBI AND MATACHEWAN DIABASE DIKES: EVIDENCE OF THE ARCHEAN GEOMAGNETIC FIELD1,2 E. IRVING AND A. J. NALDRETT Earth Physics Branch, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa and Department of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto ABSTRACT Paleomagnetic results are described from three Archean rock units, and two sets of diabase dikes that intrude them. The magnetization of the country rocks is reset by intrusion of the diabase up to distances of about 80 m from contacts. The temperature reached during intrusion at this distance determined from thermal demagnetization is about 400°C, which is also the approximate temperature predicted from Jaeger's cooling curves assuming intrusion into cool rock. At greater distances other and presumably older magnetizations are found with a westerly direction. The oldest dykes (the Matachewan) have an age of - 2.6 Ga so that this westerly directed magnetization was acquired during the Archean. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wanderin

westerly directed magnetization was acquired during the Archean. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wandering curve for the late Archean and early Aphebian which is referred to as Track 6. Track 6 has a simple form, and there is no indication that the horizontal mobility of the crust in the late Archean was any greater than during the Proterozoic. Berg ob- tained some consistent magnetization directions, but the layering at his sites is approximately uniform so that it is not possible to use Graham's fold test (Graham 1949) to determine whether the magnetiza- tion was acquired before or after deforma- tion. Berg believed that the magnetization was acquired before deformation. It is equally possible that the magnetization was acquired after deformation. INTRODUCTION The purpose of this paper is to describe new paleomagnetic results from the Abitibi Greenstone Belt, and then to use them to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) for late Archean and early Aphe- bian time (approximately -2.3 to -2.8 Ga, Ga = 109y). This polar path is of potential importance for stratigraphic correlations and for the tectonic history of late Archean

study of palaeo- magnetism of Archean rocks of Laurentia was made by Berg (1970) on the Stillwater Igneous Complex. Estimates of the age of emplacement of the complex have been obtained by Nunes and Tilton (1971) who obtained -2.75 Ga by the U-Pb method from zircons in the basal zone, and by Mueller and Wooden (1976) who obtained -2.75 + 0.05 Ga for an Rb-Sr isochron from the contact aureole. (Rb-Sr ages in this paper are quoted for SRb decay constant of 1.39 x 10-11y-1.) Berg ob- tained some consistent magnetization directions, but the layering at his sites is approximately uniform so that it is not possible to use Graham's fold test (Graham 1949) to determine whether the magnetiza- tion was acquired before or after deforma- tion. Berg believed that the magnetization was acquired before deformation. It is equally possible that the magnetization was acquired after deformation. For example the thick Archean sills of the Chibougamau Greenstone Belt have mag- netizations which structural evidence shows were acquired after deformation (Ueno and Irving 1976). METHODS Samples were cored by gasoline drill and oriented by magnetic and solar compass. About five cores were drilled at each collecting site, and two cylindrical speci- mens were cut from each core. The remanent magnetization of the specimens was measured by spinner magnetometers. All specimens were demagnetized by step-wise heating, or by alternating fields (a.f. peak field strength are quoted) using the apparatus described by Roy et al. (1969, 1971, 1973). Demagnetization was carried in fields of less than two gammas. In some samples, particularly from the Dundonald sill, no coherent magnetization could be found; if the directions in specimens from the same sample disagreed by more than 40°, the results were rejected. Eight percent of samples collected were rejected on this basis. Results from each specimen are averaged to give means for each core. The core means are averaged giving each unit weight to obtain the mean for each sampling site. The overall averages for each rock unit are calculated giving unit weight to the mean of each sampling site. ABITIBI DIKES In their unaltered state these

study of palaeo- magnetism of Archean rocks of Laurentia was made by Berg (1970) on the Stillwater Igneous Complex. Estimates of the age of emplacement of the complex have been obtained by Nunes and Tilton (1971) who obtained -2.75 Ga by the U-Pb method from zircons in the basal zone, and by Mueller and Wooden (1976) who obtained -2.75 + 0.05 Ga for an Rb-Sr isochron from the contact aureole. (Rb-Sr ages in this paper are quoted for SRb decay constant of 1.39 x 10-11y-1.) Berg ob- tained some consistent magnetization directions, but the layering at his sites is approximately uniform so that it is not possible to use Graham's fold test (Graham 1949) to determine whether the magnetiza- tion was acquired before or after deforma- tion. Ueno and Irving therefore considered these magnetizations to be somewhat younger than the Kenoran Orogeny, which in this area is determined by Rb-Sr isochrons to be about -2.6 Ga (Jones et al. 1974). NALDRETT Earth Physics Branch, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa and Department of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto ABSTRACT Paleomagnetic results are described from three Archean rock units, and two sets of diabase dikes that intrude them. The magnetization of the country rocks is reset by intrusion of the diabase up to distances of about 80 m from contacts. The temperature reached during intrusion at this distance determined from thermal demagnetization is about 400°C, which is also the approximate temperature predicted from Jaeger's cooling curves assuming intrusion into cool rock. At greater distances other and presumably older magnetizations are found with a westerly direction. The oldest dykes (the Matachewan) have an age of - 2.6 Ga so that this westerly directed magnetization was acquired during the Archean. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wandering curve for the late Archean and early Aphebian which is referred to as Track 6. Track 6 has a simple form, and there is no indication that the horizontal mobility of the crust in the late Archean was any greater than during the Proterozoic. INTRODUCTION The purpose of this paper is to describe new paleomagnetic results from the Abitibi Greenstone Belt, and then to use them to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) for late Archean and early Aphe- bian time (approximately -2.3 to -2.8 Ga, Ga = 109y). This polar path is of potential importance for stratigraphic correlations and for the tectonic history of late Archean time. For instance, it would provide information relating to the nature of the Kenoran Orogeny. Sampling was carried out during the summers of 1970, 1971, and 1973. The Abitibi greenstone belt is relatively weakly metamorphosed, the grade of metamorphism varying from lower green- schist to prehnite-pumpellyite facies (

d survive the prehnite-pumpellyite and low greenschist facies metamorphism provided there has been no chemical change of the iron minerals. It ought to be possible to retrieve original magnetizations in the Abitibi Greenstone Belt provided that magnetizations with high discrete blocking temperatures (that is square-shouldered thermal decay curves) can be located. The key observations required are the thermal decay characteristics. The metamorphism associated with the Kenoran Orogeny, is however not the only possible cause of remagnetization. Long- term mild reheating may have accom- panied either the intrusion of Proterozoic dikes, or burial beneath Huronian sedi- ments which may once have blanketed this area. Thus studies of dike contacts have been made, and one of the by- products of this work has been that we have been able to show, for the first time, that the characteristic magnetization di- rections of the Abitibi and Matachewan dike swarms were acquired at the time they were intruded. OF KAMINAK DIKES 205 1 have no expression on aeromagnetic maps. The characteristic plagioclase phenocrysts range in size from a few millimetres to 5 cm or more. Generally they constitute a very few percent of the diabase, but locally they are crowded into zones parallel to the dike walls. Within the central part of the Kaminak Sub- province, the diabase dikes range from entirely fresh to partly or wholly altered. The fresh diabase dikes have dark, charcoal gray, chilled margins with microphenocrysts of clear plagio- clase and augite, and dark gray, medium grained cores with ophitic texture and glassy plagioclase phenocrysts. In thin section, clear plagioclase laths are seen to be partly enclosed by both augite and pigeonite. Early crystallized olivine is usually present in small amounts. Thin rims of brown hornblende border pyroxene grains locally. Quartz is absent. Opaque oxide grains are chiefly Ti-magnetite-ilmenite inter- growth; skeletal ilmenite grains are uncommon. In contrast, the more completely altered diabase dikes have greenish gray chilled margins and darker greenish gray, medium grained cores with clouded, dull white or yellow plagioclase phenocrysts. Thin sections reveal a variety of alteration products, although the original ophitic texture is usua

ellyite have been identified. In the central part of the Kaminak Sub- province, the distribution of fresh and altered dikes is apparently haphazard. Both fresh and altered dikes may occur in the same outcrop area, and fresh dikes may become altered along strike. To the north and south all the dikes become altered, and can be traced through zones of increasingly higher-grade metamorphic assemblages and structural degradation to where they are reduced to large boudins of amphibo- lite within migmatitic gneisses. The heavy dashed line in Fig. 1 delimits the first obvious metamor- phic effect; primary pyroxene has not been found in thin sections of diabase north of this line, nor has the metamorphic mineral stilpno- melane been found south of it. Sampling for the current paleomagnetic study was restricted to the area in Fig. 1 south of this line. Although many of the diabase dikes south of this line are altered, it seems likely that some, if not most, of this alteration was the result of deuteric hydration during original cooling, rather than being solely an effect of Hudsonian metamor- phism. The occurrence of secondary hydrous minerals in the altered diabases that would form only at higher metamorphic grade than the first appearance of stilpnomelane is evidence in th

may be due to greater susceptibility for argon loss from previously altered dikes than from fresh ones, or it may be due to variation in the amount of low grade recrystallization during the Hudsonian. Lamprophyre Dikes Gray lamprophyres with biotite phenocrysts occur as narrow dikes, generally less than 2 m wide, throughout the region from Hudson Bay to Lake Athabaska. In the Kaminak Sub- province, the lamprophyre dikes trend between north 70" east and south 60" east. They are commonly sinuous in detail, or form very narrow swarms of discontinuous dikelets. In several places they are full of rounded country rock xenoliths. In thin sections, the lamprophyre is seen to be composed primarily of K-feldspar and biotite with lesser amounts of quartz, albite, and pale amphibole, and accessory sphene, apatite, and calcite. The larger biotite pheno- crysts have colorless (phlogopitic?) cores and orange-brown frayed rims, and are commonly bent. Lamprophyre dikes cut all rock units within the area, with the exception of the northwest- trending Mackenzie diabase dikes. Unmeta- morphosed lamprophyre dikes cut cleanly across metamorphosed Kaminak dikes, now amphibolites with granular plagioclase augen in place of primary phenocrysts, in the vicinity of O'Neil Lake (Fig. 1).

Generally they constitute a very few percent of the diabase, but locally they are crowded into zones parallel to the dike walls. Within the central part of the Kaminak Sub- province, the diabase dikes range from entirely fresh to partly or wholly altered. The fresh diabase dikes have dark, charcoal gray, chilled margins with microphenocrysts of clear plagio- clase and augite, and dark gray, medium grained cores with ophitic texture and glassy plagioclase phenocrysts. In thin section, clear plagioclase laths are seen to be partly enclosed by both augite and pigeonite. Early crystallized olivine is usually present in small amounts. Thin rims of brown hornblende border pyroxene grains locally. Quartz is absent. Opaque oxide grains are chiefly Ti-magnetite-ilmenite inter- growth; skeletal ilmenite grains are uncommon. In contrast, the more completely altered diabase dikes have greenish gray chilled margins and darker greenish gray, medium grained cores with clouded, dull white or yellow plagioclase phenocrysts. Both fresh and altered dikes may occur in the same outcrop area, and fresh dikes may become altered along strike. To the north and south all the dikes become altered, and can be traced through zones of increasingly higher-grade metamorphic assemblages and structural degradation to where they are reduced to large boudins of amphibo- lite within migmatitic gneisses. The heavy dashed line in Fig. 1 delimits the first obvious metamor- phic effect; primary pyroxene has not been found in thin sections of diabase north of this line, nor has the metamorphic mineral stilpno- melane been found south of it. Sampling for the current paleomagnetic study was restricted to the area in Fig. 1 south of this line. Although many of the diabase dikes south of this line are altered, it seems likely that some, if not most, of this alteration was the result of deuteric hydration during original cooling, rather than being solely an effect of Hudsonian metamor- phism. The occurrence of secondary hydrous minerals in the altered diabases that would form only at higher metamorphic grade than the first appearance of stilpnomelane is evidence in th

may be due to greater susceptibility for argon loss from previously altered dikes than from fresh ones, or it may be due to variation in the amount of low grade recrystallization during the Hudsonian. Lamprophyre Dikes Gray lamprophyres with biotite phenocrysts occur as narrow dikes, generally less than 2 m wide, throughout the region from Hudson Bay to Lake Athabaska. In the Kaminak Sub- province, the lamprophyre dikes trend between north 70" east and south 60" east. They are commonly sinuous in detail, or form very narrow swarms of discontinuous dikelets. In several places they are full of rounded country rock xenoliths. In thin sections, the lamprophyre is seen to be composed primarily of K-feldspar and biotite with lesser amounts of quartz, albite, and pale amphibole, and accessory sphene, apatite, and calcite. The larger biotite pheno- crysts have colorless (phlogopitic?) cores and orange-brown frayed rims, and are commonly bent. Lamprophyre dikes cut all rock units within the area, with the exception of the northwest- trending Mackenzie diabase dikes. Unmeta- morphosed lamprophyre dikes cut cleanly across metamorphosed Kaminak dikes, now amphibolites with granular plagioclase augen in place of primary phenocrysts, in the vicinity of O'Neil Lake (Fig. 1).

Generally they constitute a very few percent of the diabase, but locally they are crowded into zones parallel to the dike walls. Within the central part of the Kaminak Sub- province, the diabase dikes range from entirely fresh to partly or wholly altered. The fresh diabase dikes have dark, charcoal gray, chilled margins with microphenocrysts of clear plagio- clase and augite, and dark gray, medium grained cores with ophitic texture and glassy plagioclase phenocrysts. In contrast, the more completely altered diabase dikes have greenish gray chilled margins and darker greenish gray, medium grained cores with clouded, dull white or yellow plagioclase phenocrysts. Both fresh and altered dikes may occur in the same outcrop area, and fresh dikes may become altered along strike. To the north and south all the dikes become altered, and can be traced through zones of increasingly higher-grade metamorphic assemblages and structural degradation to where they are reduced to large boudins of amphibo- lite within migmatitic gneisses. The heavy dashed line in Fig. 1 delimits the first obvious metamor- phic effect; primary pyroxene has not been found in thin sections of diabase north of this line, nor has the metamorphic mineral stilpno- melane been found south of it. Sampling for the current paleomagnetic study was restricted to the area in Fig. 1 south of this line. Although many of the diabase dikes south of this line are altered, it seems likely that some, if not most, of this alteration was the result of deuteric hydration during original cooling, rather than being solely an effect of Hudsonian metamor- phism. The occurrence of secondary hydrous minerals in the altered diabases that would form only at higher metamorphic grade than the first appearance of stilpnomelane is evidence in th

may be due to greater susceptibility for argon loss from previously altered dikes than from fresh ones, or it may be due to variation in the amount of low grade recrystallization during the Hudsonian. Lamprophyre Dikes Gray lamprophyres with biotite phenocrysts occur as narrow dikes, generally less than 2 m wide, throughout the region from Hudson Bay to Lake Athabaska. In the Kaminak Sub- province, the lamprophyre dikes trend between north 70" east and south 60" east. They are commonly sinuous in detail, or form very narrow swarms of discontinuous dikelets. In several places they are full of rounded country rock xenoliths. In thin sections, the lamprophyre is seen to be composed primarily of K-feldspar and biotite with lesser amounts of quartz, albite, and pale amphibole, and accessory sphene, apatite, and calcite. The larger biotite pheno- crysts have colorless (phlogopitic?) cores and orange-brown frayed rims, and are commonly bent. Lamprophyre dikes cut all rock units within the area, with the exception of the northwest- trending Mackenzie diabase dikes. Unmeta- morphosed lamprophyre dikes cut cleanly across metamorphosed Kaminak dikes, now amphibolites with granular plagioclase augen in place of primary phenocrysts, in the vicinity of O'Neil Lake (Fig. 1).

Primary biotite, commonly in asso- ciation with Fe-Ti oxides, is invariably present and lesser amounts of accessory apatite are com- monly present. Primary biotite, commonly in asso- ciation with Fe-Ti oxides, is invariably present and lesser amounts of accessory apatite are com- monly present. The abundant olivine and the minor, but ever present, biotite are the min- eralogical expressions of the alkali olivine basalt chemistry of these rocks. Sudbury Diabases of. the Southern Province in- cluding the McGregor Bay Dikes These dike rocks usually display an ophitic to subophitic texture and consist of the following three major primary minerals in descending order of abundance: plagioclase of interme- diate composition, titaniferous augite (1.5-2.0% TiO, as determined by microprobe analysis), and olivine. Primary biotite, commonly in asso- ciation with Fe-Ti oxides, is invariably present and lesser amounts of accessory apatite are com- monly present. The abundant olivine and the minor, but ever present, biotite are the min- eralogical expressions of the alkali olivine basalt chemistry of these rocks. Many of the slides examined show no evidence of late stage deu- teric alteration or later regional metamorphism; many of the olivines are completely unserpentin- ized. Where there is evidence of secondary al- teration this most commonly is the partial or complete transformation of olivines to serpen- tine-chlorite-oxide minerals or to serpentine- talc-oxide minerals. Nine samples were too weak to measure using the equipment then avail- able. Specimens from the remaining six samples (all collected along the Old Hastings Road which bisects the body) were demagnetized in peak alter- nating fields of 125 Oe (1.0 x lo4 Alm). In the present study, sampling was extended throughout the body (Fig. 2). One hundred-samples from 15 sites were oriented using a Brunton mag- netic compass and cored in the laboratory. Three or more specimens from each sample were cleaned by stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization (8-12 steps) to 1OOOOe (8.0 x lo4 Alm) or by step- wise thermal demagnetization (10-13 steps) to 600°C. AF demagnetization was carried out succes- sively along three perpendicular axes using a com- mercial demagnetizer. Thermal studies were con- ducted in a noninductive furnace whose tempera- ture could be held within +3"C for 1 h. Helmholtz coils were used to cancel the earth's magnetic field to 0.5%. Sample positions were reversed for each successive step in the thermal demagnetization process to ensure that no systematic remanence was introduced due to this residual field. lti-component paleomagnetic remanences are reported for the Thanet gabbro complex of the Grenville Province in Ontario. Forty-five samples (10 sites) attain stable reversed (A) direc- tions in AF's (alternating fields) of 1500e (1.2 x lo4 A/m) or less. Blocking temperatures (TB's) are 300-350°C (5 sites) and 525-56O0(5 sites). The A, paleopole of 158.4"E, 38.03 (k = 593, a,, = 3.1") for the low TB sites differs significantly at the 95% confidence level from the A, pole of 172.0°E, 32.3"s (k = 151, a,, = 6.2") for the high TB sites. Directions from 18 additional samples (at 8 sites) follow great circle paths towards the A direction upon AF demagnetization to 1OOOOe (8.0 x lo4 Alm). TB's of the lower coercivity (B) component are 560-58O0C, above TB's of both A components. Upon thermal demagnetization, directions swing away from the A direction and endpoints reached above 560°C define a normal B paleopole at 159.3'E, 20.3"N (k = 9.6, a,, = 11.7"). If the A and B components are both of thermal origin, B predates A, and was overprinted by A during a regional metamorphic event which reset components with TB's < 560°C but left those unaffected with TB's > 560°C. The difference in the A, and A, directions represents apparent polar wander during cooling from above 500°C to less than 300°C. If

Specimens from the remaining six samples (all collected along the Old Hastings Road which bisects the body) were demagnetized in peak alter- nating fields of 125 Oe (1.0 x lo4 Alm). In the present study, sampling was extended throughout the body (Fig. 2). One hundred-samples from 15 sites were oriented using a Brunton mag- netic compass and cored in the laboratory. Three or more specimens from each sample were cleaned by stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization (8-12 steps) to 1OOOOe (8.0 x lo4 Alm) or by step- wise thermal demagnetization (10-13 steps) to 600°C. AF demagnetization was carried out succes- sively along three perpendicular axes using a com- mercial demagnetizer. Thermal studies were con- ducted in a noninductive furnace whose tempera- ture could be held within +3"C for 1 h. Helmholtz coils were used to cancel the earth's magnetic field to 0.5%. TARASIEWlCZ 1 1 Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science, MiamL Fla. 33149 (USAJ 2 Bureau de Recherches G4ologiques et Minibres, Service G~ologique National, Orleans (FranceJ Received June 10, 1976 Revised version received November 18, 1976 A series of oriented lava flows has been collected for paleomagnetic work from an axial graben situated in the Afar depression. This graben has many geophysical and structural features which suggest a similarity with the median valleys found in many mid-oceanic ridges. The results of the paleomagnetic work show that all the samples collected from the graben have normal magnetizations. This, coupled with the fact that they are obviously very young, suggests that they were emplaced during the Brunhes normal epoch of the earth's magnetic field. A series of four older lavas was sampled. These lavas gave directions just below the horizontal, but with easterly declina- tions. These directions could have been caused by a deviation of the earth's field from its normal axial dipole direction, or they could be caused by large-scale rotation about a vertical axis. This rotation could be connected to the distortion necessary to close up the continental portions of crust aro

anic type of structure. One of the most con- vincing pieces of evidence is that described by Searle [6] who studied the dispersion of surface waves travelling across the depression. He found that 274 most models gave a P-wave velocity of over 7 km/s (anomalous mantle) at depths of about 15-17 kin, thus making Afar intermediate in structure between continental type and oceanic type. Even the surficial features of tile area in which the paleomagnetic study was made, between Ghoubbat-al-Kharab and Lake Asal, have many similarities to mid-oceanic median valleys [1,7]. Volcanic activity in the area under investigation is of fissural basalts, intermediate between the alkali basalts on either side of the axial graben and true oceanic tholeiites [8,9]. This age assignment results in the Grenville poles defining an additional pre-1200-m.y, loop in the polar wander path, unrepresented in any rocks from the pre-Grenville region. A second model assumes an 1120-1000-m.y. age for the Grenville track, and hence essential contem- poraneity with the m

nd to dated poles of 1000-800 m.y. from Africa [26,27]. The problem of the history of the Grenville- Sveconorwegian Province, as it concerns palaeomag- netism and related geochronology, is therefore made up of two factors: (1) the ages of the Grenville and Sveconorwegian poles are not independently known, and (2) there is not a complete palaeomagnetic record for the pre-Grenville/Sveconorwegian regions from 1400 to 700 m.y., hence the ages of the Gren- ville and Sveconorwegian poles cannot be approxi- mated by comparison with dated poles. This study discusses Rb-Sr mineral age data and palaeomagnetic poles for dolerites, chiefly dykes which intrude the pre-Sveconorwegian (Svecofennian)region of Sweden;the width of the dykes (or thickness in the case of sills) ranges from 5 to 250 m, and they consist of a variety of olivine- and/or hypersthene-bearing dolerites [28]. The dykes trend consistently parallel to the Sveconorwegian Front or Schistosity Zone which separates the Sveconorwegian Province from the Svecofennian, and occur along almost its whole 700-kin length over a belt up to 150 km in width from the Front eastwards (Fig. 1). Field and laboratory methods Oriented cores 2.5 cm in diameter and 5-10 cm long were obtained by means of a portable diamond core drill. Pilot samples were sub- jected to progressive thermal demagnetization at six steps from 200 ° to 590°C (Fig. 3) for the determina- tion of intervals of stable or characteristic magnetiza- tion. Investiga- tions in Phanerozoic rocks have the goal of relating polarity zonations and poles to fossiliferous rocks in order to establish time lines and thus to obtain new information for the dating of unfossiliferous strata. Field and laboratory methods Oriented cores 2.5 cm in diameter and 5-10 cm long were obtained by means of a portable diamond core drill. Orientations were measured with compass and clinometer, read to the nearest one-half degree. Stratigrapic separations commonly were about 1/3 m or less, and in most cases one core was collected at each horizon. 54* After trimming, the natural remanent magnetiza- tion (NRM) of the cores was measured either on an air-driven spinner magnetometer having a background noise of 2 X 10 -7 emu, or on a cryogenic supercon- ducting rock magnetometer having a background noise of 1 X 10 -7 emu or less. Field and laboratory methods Oriented cores 2.5 cm in diameter and 5-10 cm long were obtained by means of a portable diamond core drill. Orientations were measured with compass and clinometer, read to the nearest one-half degree. Stratigrapic separations commonly were about 1/3 m or less, and in most cases one core was collected at each horizon. 54* After trimming, the natural remanent magnetiza- tion (NRM) of the cores was measured either on an air-driven spinner magnetometer having a background noise of 2 X 10 -7 emu, or on a cryogenic supercon- ducting rock magnetometer having a background noise of 1 X 10 -7 emu or less. Pilot samples were sub- jected to progressive thermal demagnetization at six steps from 200 ° to 590°C (Fig. 3) for the determina- tion of intervals of stable or characteristic magnetiza- tion. Thermal demagnetization analysis was employed because the remanent magnetization resides prin- cipally in hematite, whose magnetic coercivity is very high. The objects of this paper are two-fold, firstly to obtain chemical, petrographic and palaeomagnetic data from the Montagnais dikes and, secondly, to derive a pole position for them from stability tested data. Since palaeomagnetism takes a greater importance in determining the time order of Pre- cambrian rocks and in studying the nature of Precambrian orogenesis, many detailed palaeomagnetic studies ought to be conducted in order to determine the variations of the Precambrian geomagnetic field. This work is a small contribution to this general requirement, but it is of some interest since no definite trend of apparent polar wandering has yet been established for the 1000-1500 m.y. span. Methods applied The sampling for this study was made by collecting oriented hand samples at an average rate of five per outcrop, mainly from natural outcrops. From the 33 sampling localities which are listed with relevant data in Table 1 those numbered N1, N2,..., N24 with the exception of N5 and N16 represent Younger Granite occurrences. N5, N16 and N25-N31 are localities in the youngest volcanics, while N32 and N33 refer to two Cretaceous outcrops. Within each locality samples are numbered by additional numerals separated by a hyphen from the symbol of locality, e.g. N4-2 means the second sample of locality N4. A.C. demagnetization technique was applied and the measurements of magnetiza- tion were carried out with a high sensitivity JR-2 (Jelinek) spinner-, and a low sensi- tivity home-made astatic magnetometer, respectively. Data processing was made on a RAZDAN-3 computer. Both measurements and data processing were executed in Hungary using the instruments and facilities of the Department of Geophysics, E/StvSs University, Budapest. Methods applied The sampling for this study was made by collecting oriented hand samples at an average rate of five per outcrop, mainly from natural outcrops. From the 33 sampling localities which are listed with relevant data in Table 1 those numbered N1, N2,..., N24 with the exception of N5 and N16 represent Younger Granite occurrences. N5, N16 and N25-N31 are localities in the youngest volcanics, while N32 and N33 refer to two Cretaceous outcrops. Within each locality samples are numbered by additional numerals separated by a hyphen from the symbol of locality, e.g. N4-2 means the second sample of locality N4. A.C. demagnetization technique was applied and the measurements of magnetiza- tion were carried out with a high sensitivity JR-2 (Jelinek) spinner-, and a low sensi- tivity home-made astatic magnetometer, respectively. Data processing was made on a RAZDAN-3 computer. Both measurements and data processing were executed in Hungary using the instruments and facilities of the Department of Geophysics, E/StvSs University, Budapest. Ore microscopy The results of microscopic observations made on 25 samples from 21 localities, N1-N22 (except N4) are presented in Table 2.
